::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .53", "p = .99", "p = .87", "p = .442" ), Sentence = c("Acceptance rates were comparable between the groups (0.719 in the low depressivesymptom group and 0.703 in the high depressive-symptom group; t(324) = -0.62, p = .53, d = -0.07).", "Higher CES-D total scores went with longer median response times (r(349) = 0.23, p < .001), but were uncorrelated with acceptance rates (r(349) = .00, p = .99).", "The contrast weight differed little between the groups (low CES-D = 0.29 vs high CES-D = 0.24, t(332) = 0.17, p = .87, d = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.19, 0.23]).", "With the threshold, nondecision time, mean-signal drift, and median response time as covariates, the adjusted delay was 0.08 s (95% CI [-0.12, 0.28], p = .442, BF01 = 3.38; Supplement S4, Fig. S2a)." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. We examined 581 columns across 54 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 54 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Depression is often characterized by reduced reward sensitivity, slowed responding, and altered social functioning.
Prior drift-diffusion modeling studies have linked depression to less efficient accumulation of decision evidence and to greater decision caution in non-social decision-making tasks.

However, it remains unclear whether similar process-level alterations extend to social decision-making tasks, such as the ultimatum game, which involves weighing monetary reward against emotional reactions to another player's offer.

To address this question, we applied drift-diffusion models to a publicly available dataset in which 351 adults, grouped by the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), responded to offers in the ultimatum game.
Participants with elevated depressive symptoms accepted offers at a rate comparable to those with lower symptoms but responded more slowly.

In a standard timestationary diffusion model, the high depressive-symptom group showed weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, indexed by lower drift rate and wider decision thresholds, respectively.
In an exploratory time-varying model that allowed different attributes to enter the decision process at different times, the same group differences in drift rate and decision threshold were observed.
Additionally, the difference between reward and emotion information was estimated to enter the decision process later in the high depressive-symptom group.

These findings suggest that depression-related slowing during social decision-making may arise from weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, which are not apparent from acceptance rates alone.
Depression is a common and burdensome mental health condition, affecting an estimated 3.4% of the global population (GBD 2019 Mental Disorders Collaborators, 2022).
text.formatted: Depression is a common and burdensome mental health condition, affecting an estimated 3.4% of the global population <ref type="bibr">(GBD 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mental Disorders Collaborators, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: It is characterized by persistent low mood and loss of interest in rewarding activities, and these symptoms are associated with changes in reward processing and social functioning.

Indeed, people with depression show impaired reward processing across behavioral tasks (Halahakoon et al., 2020) and often respond more slowly, consistent with psychomotor retardation as a core clinical feature of the disorder (Bennabi et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Indeed, people with depression show impaired reward processing across behavioral tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Halahakoon et al., 2020)</ref> and often respond more slowly, consistent with psychomotor retardation as a core clinical feature of the disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bennabi et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Depression is also associated with substantial social impairment.

Individuals with depression report greater perceived social disability than controls, and this difference can persist after remission and predict diagnostic status two years later (Saris et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Individuals with depression report greater perceived social disability than controls, and this difference can persist after remission and predict diagnostic status two years later <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Saris et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Economic games, such as the ultimatum game, provide controlled paradigms for studying impairments related to social decision-making (Kupferberg et al., 2016; Güth et al., 1982).
text.formatted: Economic games, such as the ultimatum game, provide controlled paradigms for studying impairments related to social decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Kupferberg et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Güth et al., 1982)</ref>.

text.text: In the ultimatum game, a proposer offers to split a sum of money with a responder.
If the responder accepts, both players receive the proposed amounts, and if the responder rejects, neither player receives any money (Güth et al., 1982).
text.formatted: If the responder accepts, both players receive the proposed amounts, and if the responder rejects, neither player receives any money <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Güth et al., 1982)</ref>.

text.text: Rejecting an unfair offer therefore costs the responder the amount offered. Güth et al. (1982) interpreted the rejection of unfair offers as punishment of a proposer who demands too much.
text.formatted: Rejecting an unfair offer therefore costs the responder the amount offered. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Güth et al. (1982)</ref> interpreted the rejection of unfair offers as punishment of a proposer who demands too much.

text.text: This choice requires integrating material payoff with fairness-related and emotional responses.
In this game, emotion prediction errors predicted the rejection of offers in addition to reward prediction errors (Heffner et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In this game, emotion prediction errors predicted the rejection of offers in addition to reward prediction errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Heffner et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Feelings about each outcome also updated expected value across trials in a trust game and a lottery task, according to the best-fitting learning model (Teoh et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Feelings about each outcome also updated expected value across trials in a trust game and a lottery task, according to the best-fitting learning model <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Teoh et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, a meta-analysis of ultimatum games in depression found significant heterogeneity in the rejection of unfair offers, leading to an insignificant pooled effect (Yin et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, a meta-analysis of ultimatum games in depression found significant heterogeneity in the rejection of unfair offers, leading to an insignificant pooled effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Yin et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Even the participants who accepted more unfair offers rated them as more disgusting and anger-provoking (Harlé et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Even the participants who accepted more unfair offers rated them as more disgusting and anger-provoking <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Harlé et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: One possibility is that overt choices may obscure differences in the valuation and affective processes that lead to them.
Depression-related changes in social decision-making therefore need to be further clarified at the level of the latent processes that combine monetary and affective information.
Drift-diffusion models (DDMs) provide a useful way to characterize the latent processes that generate choices and response times.

In these models, drift rate indexes the strength and direction of evidence accumulation, the decision threshold indexes the amount of evidence required before committing to a decision, and non-decision time indexes the duration of stimulus encoding and response execution (Ratcliff & Mckoon, 2008).
text.formatted: In these models, drift rate indexes the strength and direction of evidence accumulation, the decision threshold indexes the amount of evidence required before committing to a decision, and non-decision time indexes the duration of stimulus encoding and response execution <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ratcliff & Mckoon, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Previous reward-based decisionmaking studies suggest that depression is associated with lower drift rates and wider decision threshold, whereas non-decision time is comparable to that of controls (Lawlor et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Previous reward-based decisionmaking studies suggest that depression is associated with lower drift rates and wider decision threshold, whereas non-decision time is comparable to that of controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lawlor et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Shen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, this evidence comes mainly from the probabilistic reward task and other non-social paradigms.
In the ultimatum game, participants above a conventional cutoff for depressive symptoms responded more slowly than participants below it (Fu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In the ultimatum game, participants above a conventional cutoff for depressive symptoms responded more slowly than participants below it <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Fu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: It remains unclear whether this slowing reflects weaker evidence accumulation, greater decision caution, longer non-decision time, or some combination of these processes.
A slower decision may also reflect differences in when distinct sources of information begin to influence evidence accumulation.
Standard DDMs assume that evidence from each decision attribute is available from the start of accumulation and exerts a constant influence within a trial.

However, recent work suggests that attributes can enter the accumulation process at different times, making relative onset time a decision parameter separable from the weight assigned to an attribute. (Maier et al., 2020; Sullivan & Huettel, 2021).
text.formatted: However, recent work suggests that attributes can enter the accumulation process at different times, making relative onset time a decision parameter separable from the weight assigned to an attribute. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Maier et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Sullivan & Huettel, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Time-varying DDMs estimate these onset times from choices and response times and have recently been applied to social decision-making.
For example, relative social status shifted attribute onset time in altruistic choice while leaving attribute weights largely unchanged (Ni & Li, 2025).
text.formatted: For example, relative social status shifted attribute onset time in altruistic choice while leaving attribute weights largely unchanged <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ni & Li, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In another social decision-making study, a secondary attribute of the choice influenced behavior later than the primary one (Wittmann et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In another social decision-making study, a secondary attribute of the choice influenced behavior later than the primary one <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Wittmann et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Time-varying DDMs may also offer mechanistic insight into clinical symptoms.

For example, in a food-choice study, induced negative affect shifted the onset of taste relative to health information more strongly in women with bulimia nervosa than in controls (Shevlin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, in a food-choice study, induced negative affect shifted the onset of taste relative to health information more strongly in women with bulimia nervosa than in controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Shevlin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the ultimatum game, depressive symptoms may therefore alter not only how strongly monetary and emotional information influence decision-making, but also when these sources of information enter the decision process.
Whether the relative onset time of reward-and emotion-related information varies with depressive symptoms remains an open question.
Here, we used a computational modeling approach to test whether slower social decisions in people with elevated depressive symptoms reflect weaker evidence accumulation, greater caution, or both.
In an exploratory analysis, we also estimated when the difference between reward and emotion signals began to influence these decisions.
We applied time-stationary and time-varying DDMs to a publicly available dataset in which 351 adults responded to offers in the ultimatum game (Heffner et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We applied time-stationary and time-varying DDMs to a publicly available dataset in which 351 adults responded to offers in the ultimatum game <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Heffner et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Each offer was associated with trial-level reward and emotion prediction errors.
Since these two prediction errors are correlated across trials, the design supports inferences about their shared and differentiating components rather than about reward or emotion separately.
We therefore decomposed them into a mean signal and a contrast signal.
In the time-stationary model, the mean signal drives evidence accumulation throughout the trial.
We compared its drift rate and the decision threshold between participants above and below the conventional cutoff for depressive symptoms.
For this exploratory analysis, we specified a time-varying model so that the mean signal drives evidence accumulation from the beginning and the contrast signal enters after an onset time.
We compared the estimated onset time between the two groups and also tested its association with symptom severity across the full sample.
We used publicly available data from Experiment 4 of Heffner et al. (2021), which included 351 adults.
text.formatted: We used publicly available data from Experiment 4 of <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Heffner et al. (2021)</ref>, which included 351 adults.

text.text: Participants were divided into two groups based on their Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) score.

Of these, 205 scored below the conventional cutoff of 16 (low depressive-symptom group) and 146 scored at or above it (high depressive-symptom group), following the classification of Heffner et al. (2021).
text.formatted: Of these, 205 scored below the conventional cutoff of 16 (low depressive-symptom group) and 146 scored at or above it (high depressive-symptom group), following the classification of <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Heffner et al. (2021)</ref>.

The ultimatum game is a classical social decision-making task, in which two players interact to divide a sum of money (Güth et al., 1982; Güth & Kocher, 2014).

text.text: Participants played as the responder.
On each trial, they decided whether to accept or reject a monetary offer from a proposer.

Before receiving the offer, participants predicted the amount they expected to receive and rated their predicted feelings about the exchange; after receiving the offer, they rated their experienced feelings.
The task yields two trial-level prediction-error signals per offer.
The reward prediction error is the received minus the predicted monetary amount, whereas the emotion prediction error is the experienced minus the predicted valence rating.
We used the valence prediction error only and did not enter the arousal prediction error in any model.
Valence prediction errors predicted social choices across task contexts, whereas the effect of arousal prediction errors depended on the context (Heffner et al., 2021).

text.text: Each was divided by a single standard deviation computed over all trials pooled across the participants, without mean-centering.
We split each trial's two prediction errors into the part they share and the part on which they diverge, their mean and their contrast.
Across trials the two standardized signals are strongly correlated (r = .757), so their separate drift weights compete for the same variance.
Because each prediction error is standardized to unit variance over the pooled data, the mean and the contrast are uncorrelated across that pooled sample, however strongly RPE and EPE are correlated.

We modeled choice and response time jointly with a drift-diffusion process, in which noisy evidence accumulates until it reaches one of two boundaries (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008).
text.formatted: We modeled choice and response time jointly with a drift-diffusion process, in which noisy evidence accumulates until it reaches one of two boundaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence starts between the boundaries, accumulates at a mean rate (i.e., the drift rate), and the first boundary reached determines both the choice and its latency.
We assigned acceptance to the upper boundary and rejection to the lower, so that a positive drift indexes a propensity to accept.

The primary parameters compared between groups are drift rate,which indexes the rate and direction of evidence accumulation, and decision threshold, which indexes the evidence required before committing to a choice.
The model also estimates non-decision time, which is defined as the response time spent on stimulus encoding and motor execution outside the decision process.

We fitted the model by evaluating the joint likelihood of choice and response time deterministically using the Navarro-Fuss series for the Wiener first-passage-time density (Navarro & Fuss, 2009), rather than by simulating the diffusion process.
text.formatted: We fitted the model by evaluating the joint likelihood of choice and response time deterministically using the Navarro-Fuss series for the Wiener first-passage-time density <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Navarro & Fuss, 2009)</ref>, rather than by simulating the diffusion process.

text.text: A deterministic likelihood avoids the Monte-Carlo noise in the likelihood surface, which is especially important when each participant contributes relatively few trials.
To keep the remaining parameters identifiable, we fixed several quantities.

The starting point was fixed at the unbiased midpoint (Voss et al., 2015), the diffusion coefficient σ was fixed at 1.4 as a scaling convention, and across-trial variability in drift rate, starting point, and nondecision time was fixed to zero.

text.text: This study used DDM to examine the decision processes underlying slower social decisions in people with elevated depressive symptoms.
We found that although acceptance rates were comparable between the groups, the high depressive-symptom group responded more slowly.
In the time-stationary DDM, the high depressive-symptom group showed reduced sensitivity to the mean reward-emotion signal and a wider decision threshold.
The time-varying model yielded the same pattern for both parameters.
In an exploratory analysis, depressive symptoms were associated with a later estimated onset of the reward-emotion contrast signal.
Together, these findings suggest that depression-related slowing during social decision-making reflects weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution.
These results are consistent with prior evidence of response slowing during social decision-making among individuals with elevated depressive symptoms (Fu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: These results are consistent with prior evidence of response slowing during social decision-making among individuals with elevated depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Fu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Using DDMs, previous studies have shown lower drift rates and wider thresholds among depressed participants in non-social reward tasks (Lawlor et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2024).

text.text: The present study extends this decision-process profile to social decision-making, showing lower drift rates and wider decision thresholds in an ultimatum game.
Previous work interpreted slower responding during the ultimatum game as psychomotor slowing (Fu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Previous work interpreted slower responding during the ultimatum game as psychomotor slowing <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Fu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In the present data, the slower responses went together with weaker evidence accumulation and a wider threshold.
The decision-process differences reported in non-social tasks may therefore also account for the slower responses of people with depression in social decisions.

Some recent evidence suggests that different attributes may enter decision processes at different time points (Maier et al., 2020; Sullivan & Huettel, 2021), and such onset differences may be altered in clinical populations (Shevlin et al., 2025).

text.text: We therefore conducted an exploratory time-varying DDM analysis in the current study.
In this model, the mean signal drives evidence accumulation from the beginning of the decision process, whereas the contrast signal enters after an onset time.
We found that the estimated onset of the contrast signal was later in the high depressive-symptom group than in the low depressive-symptom group.
However, this result should be treated as preliminary, since the time-varying DDM had a higher BIC than the standard DDM.

One potential issue limiting the advantage and interpretability of the time-varying model is that the reward and emotion prediction errors were highly correlated, so they could not be treated as fully independent attributes.

The mean-contrast decomposition therefore captures the shared and differentiating components of the two prediction errors, but the contrast signal varies over a narrow range, which leaves its weight and onset weakly determined in some participants (Supplement S1).

Future studies should confirm this finding in designs with more independent reward and emotion prediction-error signals, or with additional process measures that can independently validate attribute-onset timing.
These findings have several theoretical and clinical implications.
First, these results suggest that comparable choices in high and low depressive-symptom groups can arise from different latent decision processes.
In the ultimatum game, acceptance rates did not differ between groups, but DDMs indicated weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution in participants with elevated depressive symptoms.
Therefore, social decision-making in depression may be altered even when overt choices appear intact.
Second, the results refine the interpretation of depression-related response slowing.

Slower social decisions may reflect reduced efficiency in accumulating evidence and greater decision caution, rather than global psychomotor slowing alone (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008; Weigard et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Slower social decisions may reflect reduced efficiency in accumulating evidence and greater decision caution, rather than global psychomotor slowing alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Weigard et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Third, these process-level measures may serve as candidate markers for future intervention studies.

For example, interventions aimed at improving social functioning in individuals elevated depressive symptoms could examine whether these individuals show increased evidence-accumulation efficiency, reduced excessive caution, or both.

Although these applications remain preliminary, DDM parameters may help link depressive symptoms to specific cognitive processes that contribute to social impairment and may provide measurable targets for future mechanistic treatment research.
This study also has some limitations.
First, because the groups were defined by a selfreport symptom scale, the results apply to elevated depressive symptoms rather than to clinically diagnosed depression.
Second, the monetary and emotional information were available at the same time in the current task.
Mouse tracking (Maier et al., 2020) or a task that presents the two kinds of information at different times would provide an independent check of the estimated onset.

text.text: Third, the onset difference should be interpreted with caution.
The time-varying DDM did not provide a clear improvement in fit after accounting for model complexity, and individual onset estimates were not reliably recovered at the current trial count.
Thus, the onset parameter should be interpreted at the group level rather than as a stable individual-difference measure.
Finally, the neural mechanisms underlying these process-level alterations remain unclear.

Future studies could use event-related potentials or functional neuroimaging techniques to examine the neural correlates of weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution during social decision-making in individuals with elevated depressive symptoms.
In summary, this study used DDMs to examine cognitive mechanisms underlying social decision-making and their associations with depressive symptoms.
In the ultimatum game, the high depressive-symptom group responded more slowly than the low depressive-symptom group and accepted offers at a comparable rate.
Their slower responses were accompanied by a lower drift rate and a wider decision threshold, suggesting weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, respectively.
An exploratory time-varying model estimated a later onset of the reward-emotion contrast signal in the high depressive-symptom group.
We read this delay as part of a broader slowing of the decision.
Together, these results suggest that DDMs of social decision-making can elucidate the computational components underlying depression-related slowing.

Drift rate and decision threshold may provide candidate process-level mechanisms for future intervention studies aimed at improving social decision-making difficulties associated with depressive symptoms.
